ideas.idea: Editorial long-read: one 640px text column on the left, a wide right margin holding screenshots and short notes as marginalia, like a printed book page.
ideas.why: Lets the product be explained in sentences, which suits a careful buyer deciding whether to give an AI their inbox.

ideas.idea: Field manual: numbered chapters 01 to 08 with a sticky left index; each chapter ends with a small 'back to index' link.
ideas.why: Setup really is a short sequence (connect, paste URL, ask, approve), so a manual structure tells the truth about it.

ideas.idea: Sticky split: left 5 columns hold headline and Start free pinned; right 7 columns scroll through four screenshots in order (connect, paste URL, ask, approve).
ideas.why: The CTA never leaves the screen while the four real steps play out beside it.

ideas.idea: Docs-shaped homepage: left sidebar of anchors (Overview, Providers, Clients, Security, Approval, Plans), main column written like a quickstart with the connector URL in a code block.
ideas.why: Many visitors arrive from Cursor and VS Code; a docs page feels native to them and shows how little setup there is.

ideas.idea: Newspaper front page: masthead with today's date and 'Stockholm', a lead story about the draft card across 8 columns, a 4-column side rail 'Also in this edition' for providers and plans.
ideas.why: News layout carries a lot of content densely and makes the Stockholm data location part of the masthead.

ideas.idea: Catalogue index: the page opens with a stacked list of five 'titles' (Connect, Ask, Approve, Teams, Plans), each line linking down to its full section.
ideas.why: A visitor sees the whole product in five lines before reading anything, then jumps to what they care about.

ideas.idea: Technical paper: a short abstract under the H1, then numbered sections with every visual captioned 'Fig. 1', 'Fig. 2', footnotes at the end.
ideas.why: Signals rigour about security and data handling without a compliance badge.

ideas.idea: Desktop metaphor: the page is a light desktop with three overlapping windows (Inbox, Claude chat, Draft card) that can be focused by click; a plain stacked fallback on mobile.
ideas.why: Shows the three parts of the product side by side the way a user actually has them open.

ideas.idea: One continuous transcript: the whole page is a single chat thread top to bottom, with explanatory annotations in the left margin next to each message.
ideas.why: The product lives inside a chat, so the page is a chat, read like a case study.

ideas.idea: Field-guide index: providers listed as guide entries (identification: OAuth or app password; habitat: personal or company domain; notes), filterable by type.
ideas.why: Provider fit is the first question people ask; a guide answers it per provider instead of with a logo wall.

ideas.idea: Two-track page: after the hero the page forks into two parallel columns, 'For you' and 'For your team (info@, sales@)', running side by side to pricing.
ideas.why: About half of paying customers are teams on their own domain; they get their own column instead of a footnote.

ideas.idea: Changelog as body: below a short hero, the main content is recent dated changelog entries grouped by month, like a numbered newsletter archive.
ideas.why: Shows a living product without claiming numbers.

ideas.idea: Alternating rows with bleed: text in 5 left columns, screenshot in 7 columns bleeding off the right edge of the viewport, five rows.
ideas.why: A familiar reading rhythm that gives screenshots room at real size.

ideas.idea: Spec sheet: the core of the page is one long two-column key/value table (Providers, Clients, Data location, Storage, Approval, Revoke, Plans) with screenshots between table groups.
ideas.why: Technical buyers get every fact on one scan.

ideas.idea: FAQ as the page: short hero, then every question as an H2 with its answer open (no accordion), grouped Setup, Safety, Teams, Billing.
ideas.why: Objections decide this purchase; a page that is mostly answers respects that.

ideas.idea: Filled magazine grid: an asymmetric 6-column grid where every tile carries a real asset (screenshot crop, 3D object, real quote, diagram) with a caption; no empty tiles.
ideas.why: Gives the coming assets a gallery without the empty bento look.

ideas.idea: Product catalogue with plates: each plan shown as a printed catalogue plate with a large number, name, and what it includes, then a single shared CTA.
ideas.why: Pricing by inbox is simple; a plate per plan makes it scannable.

ideas.idea: The real draft card, rendered from the shipping card build at 1:1, with To, Subject, body and Approve / Edit buttons, next to a left-aligned H1.
ideas.why: Proves the strongest differentiator in the first second: nothing goes out without your yes.

ideas.idea: Before and after on one sample mailbox: left pane a raw inbox, right pane the same inbox with three AI drafts waiting, labelled 'sample mailbox'.
ideas.why: Shows the outcome, not the plumbing.

ideas.idea: A real Claude conversation screenshot: the user asks for the unpaid invoices in invoices@ and gets a short list plus drafted reminders.
ideas.why: A business task on a shared address speaks to the team half of customers.

ideas.idea: The provider list is the headline: 'Gmail. Outlook. iCloud. Fastmail. Yahoo. Zoho. Any IMAP.' set very large, each word linking to its connect guide.
ideas.why: Answers 'does it work with mine?' before anything else.

ideas.idea: The connector URL as hero: one copyable field holding the real connector URL, a Copy button, and 'Paste this into Claude or ChatGPT.'
ideas.why: Shows the setup really is one URL.

ideas.idea: Three-frame sequence: three stills left to right (Connect, Ask, Approve), the same size, captioned 1, 2, 3.
ideas.why: The whole product in one row.

ideas.idea: The draft card as a physical 3D object lying on a light desk surface, with the H1 'Nothing sends until you say so.'
ideas.why: Makes approval tangible and ownable; nobody else has this object.

ideas.idea: A question as H1: 'What did the accountant ask for last week?' with the AI's answer card under it.
ideas.why: Starts from a task people recognise instead of a category name.

ideas.idea: Install hero: two equal columns 'Add to Claude' and 'Add to ChatGPT', each with three numbered steps and a screenshot, Start free above both.
ideas.why: Most visitors already chose their AI client; meet them there.

ideas.idea: A 3D envelope with the draft pulled halfway out, a strong long shadow, H1 beside it.
ideas.why: A calm, ownable object instead of an abstract graphic.

ideas.idea: Team hero: a 3D postbox with three labelled slots (info@, sales@, invoices@) and copy aimed at small businesses on their own domain.
ideas.why: Speaks directly to the business half of payers.

ideas.idea: Type-only hero: a two-sentence statement set large, Start free under it, and the first screenshot starts right at the fold.
ideas.why: Confidence through restraint; fast to load.

ideas.idea: Data-path diagram hero: your inbox, then MCPEmails (passes through, stores nothing, Stockholm), then your AI, drawn as one clean horizontal line.
ideas.why: Answers the privacy question with a picture.

ideas.idea: Dashboard hero: a tight crop of the real dashboard with connected inboxes and recent actions, plus a 'see the draft card' secondary link.
ideas.why: Shows there is a real product and control panel behind the connector.

ideas.idea: One muted looping clip (about 12 seconds): a question typed in Claude, the draft card appears, the user clicks Approve, 'Sent' shows.
ideas.why: The whole value loop in one clip.

ideas.idea: A printed email draft with a rubber 'APPROVED' stamp and a signature line, photographed flat, H1 to its left.
ideas.why: Turns the approval step into a memorable mark.

ideas.idea: Client tabs: Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code; each tab shows that client's real screenshot doing the same task.
ideas.why: Proves 'works in your client' with real screens.

ideas.idea: Paper and ink: warm off-white paper surface, brand ink navy for all type, brand cobalt used only on actions (Start free, Approve, links).
ideas.why: Cobalt becomes a signal for 'this does something', which echoes the approve-before-send idea.

ideas.idea: Swiss rules: white ground, heavy 2px ink rules between sections, thin 1px rules inside them, cobalt only as one solid block per section.
ideas.why: Structure through rules instead of cards and shadows.

ideas.idea: Ink band: a light page with one full-width brand-ink (navy) band for the security section, cobalt and mint accents inside it, light again after.
ideas.why: A dark accent inside a light page marks the 'vault' part of the story.

ideas.idea: Pasteup board: screenshots mounted with visible paper edges and small crop marks, slight off-white board texture behind them.
ideas.why: Feels made by hand, the opposite of generic AI gloss.

ideas.idea: Blueprint grid: faint 8px grid on the page background in a very light cobalt tint, diagrams drawn in cobalt lines, screenshots unframed.
ideas.why: Technical honesty; the grid also aligns everything.

ideas.idea: Manila surfaces: alternating sections on a pale envelope-manila tint and white, type in brand ink, cobalt for links.
ideas.why: The envelope surface ties the page to mail without clip art.

ideas.idea: Quiet density: generous white space, 1px hairline borders in a light ink tint, no shadows anywhere, cobalt used under 5% of the page area.
ideas.why: A restrained surface makes real screenshots the colour on the page.

ideas.idea: Framed prints: screenshots sit on cream mats with thin ink frames like prints on a wall, captions under each in small caps.
ideas.why: Treats the product UI as the art.

ideas.idea: Marker highlight: plain black-and-white body with key phrases (never stored, you approve) highlighted in a light cobalt-soft wash, like a highlighter.
ideas.why: Draws the eye to the two promises that matter.

ideas.idea: Duotone screenshots: every screenshot converted to brand ink plus paper, except the draft card, which stays in full colour.
ideas.why: The one coloured object on the page is the one that matters.

ideas.idea: Riso texture: diagrams printed in two overlapping inks (brand cobalt and mint) with fine grain and slight misregistration.
ideas.why: Warm print texture without new colours.

ideas.idea: Museum white: pure white, objects (3D envelope, draft card) shot with soft contact shadows, grey captions, very wide spacing.
ideas.why: Calm, premium, and it makes the 3D objects feel collected rather than decorative.

ideas.idea: Hardware labels: light grey panels with tiny uppercase labels in ink and cobalt status dots, like markings on a device.
ideas.why: Gives the connector a tangible, engineered feel.

ideas.idea: Ledger lines: pricing and spec tables on faint horizontal rules like a ledger, numbers in tabular figures, cobalt totals.
ideas.why: Fits teams running invoices@ and keeps tables readable.

ideas.idea: Postmark separators: section breaks are circular postmarks in cobalt line work (date plus 'STOCKHOLM'), the only ornament on the page.
ideas.why: One ownable ornament that also carries the data-location fact.

ideas.idea: Semantic colour only: brand colours keep their product meaning everywhere (cobalt = action, mint = sent or approved, amber = held, red = blocked), nothing decorative.
ideas.why: Visitors learn the product's states just by reading the page.

ideas.idea: High-density print: smaller body (15px), tight leading, many short sections, ink rules, like a dense reference card; cobalt for headings only.
ideas.why: Rewards readers who want every detail.

ideas.idea: Fraunces 600 (opsz 144, SOFT 0) for H1 and H2, Instrument Sans 400/500 body at 18px, IBM Plex Mono 400 for email addresses and the connector URL.
ideas.why: A warm serif display with plain body text; mono marks anything you can copy.

ideas.idea: Newsreader 500 italic H1 at 72px, Newsreader 400 body at 19px, Martian Mono 400 at 12px for labels and captions.
ideas.why: Editorial, letter-like, readable at length.

ideas.idea: Instrument Serif 400 at 96px for the H1 only, Geist 400/600 for everything else, Geist Mono 400 for the connector URL.
ideas.why: One dramatic serif moment, then calm modern text.

ideas.idea: Space Grotesk 700 headings at -2% tracking, IBM Plex Sans 400 body, Space Mono 400 for addresses like info@.
ideas.why: Technical character without looking like a terminal.

ideas.idea: Schibsted Grotesk 800 headlines (a Nordic newspaper face), Source Serif 4 400 body at 18px, Schibsted Grotesk 500 small caps style for kickers.
ideas.why: Newspaper voice with a Scandinavian origin.

ideas.idea: Libre Caslon Text 400/700 for headings and body, Courier Prime 400 for To / From / Subject lines.
ideas.why: Reads like a typed letter, ties the page to correspondence.

ideas.idea: All monospace: Commit Mono 400/700 (SIL OFL) throughout, scale 14 / 18 / 32 / 64, aligned to character columns.
ideas.why: A developer-native page for Cursor and VS Code visitors.

ideas.idea: Bricolage Grotesque 800 at wdth 75 for a large condensed H1, Bricolage Grotesque 400 body at opsz 14.
ideas.why: One variable family, lots of character, self-hosts as a single file.

ideas.idea: Familjen Grotesk 600 headings (from a Stockholm foundry), Literata 400 body at 18px, Familjen Grotesk 500 for buttons.
ideas.why: Quietly ties the type to Stockholm, where the data lives.

ideas.idea: Archivo 800 at wdth 62 for poster-like headlines, Archivo 400 at wdth 100 body, same family for everything.
ideas.why: Swiss-poster energy from one variable font.

ideas.idea: Young Serif 400 headings, Hanken Grotesk 400/600 body, tabular figures for pricing.
ideas.why: Friendly, slightly old-fashioned serif that suits a calm mail product.

ideas.idea: Courier Prime 400/700 for headings set like typed memos, IBM Plex Serif 400 body.
ideas.why: Typewritten headings make every section feel like a memo.

ideas.idea: IBM Plex Sans Condensed 600 headings, IBM Plex Sans 400 body, IBM Plex Mono 400 labels: one superfamily, manual style.
ideas.why: Engineering-manual coherence with zero pairing risk.

ideas.idea: Source Serif 4 600 at opsz 60 for a 72px display, Public Sans 400 body, Public Sans 700 for labels.
ideas.why: Government-plain body under a confident serif.

ideas.idea: Geist 500 everywhere with a capped scale (15 / 20 / 40px); the H1 is only 40px.
ideas.why: Quiet typography so screenshots and the draft card lead.

ideas.idea: Spectral 300 italic for large display lines, Work Sans 400/500 body.
ideas.why: Light, literary display without heaviness.

ideas.idea: Atkinson Hyperlegible 400/700 for headings and body, DM Mono 400 for addresses.
ideas.why: Legibility as a value, good for an audience that reads carefully.

ideas.idea: Gloock 400 high-contrast headlines, Chivo 400 body, Chivo Mono 400 labels.
ideas.why: Strong editorial contrast in headings, sober body text.

ideas.idea: Problem first: 'Your AI can write the email. It still can't send it.' Then the fix, then the proof.
ideas.why: Names the friction every Claude or ChatGPT user knows.

ideas.idea: Demo first: the page opens with a full task walkthrough, and explanation only starts after it.
ideas.why: People believe what they see working.

ideas.idea: Objections first: the first section after the hero answers three worries (Will it send without me? Is my mail stored? Does it work with my provider?) with proof for each.
ideas.why: These worries are what stop signups; answer them before features.

ideas.idea: By hand versus connected: the same task shown twice, once copying between inbox and chat, once with MCPEmails.
ideas.why: Compares against the real alternative (doing it yourself), not competitors.

ideas.idea: Use cases by mailbox: invoices@, sales@, info@ and a personal inbox, each a short story with one screenshot.
ideas.why: Business addresses are where half the paying customers live.

ideas.idea: Day in the life: morning triage, midday replies, end-of-day follow-ups, each with a real task and the draft card.
ideas.why: Shows the habit, not a one-off trick.

ideas.idea: Chain of custody: follow one email from the provider, through MCPEmails, to the AI, to the draft card, to sent, stating what touches it at each step.
ideas.why: Turns the security model into a story.

ideas.idea: Founder letter: why the product exists and what it promises, signed, with features as a short P.S. list.
ideas.why: A small company's best proof is a real person.

ideas.idea: Beliefs: numbered principles (mail is fetched live, you approve sends, your provider stays the source of truth) each backed by a link to how it works.
ideas.why: A clear point of view on agents and email.

ideas.idea: Agent's-eye view: the page narrates what the AI can see and do once connected, and where it has to stop and ask.
ideas.why: Makes permissions concrete and reassuring.

ideas.idea: A team story: one small business, three shared addresses, who asks the AI and who approves, ending on Business per person.
ideas.why: Sells the Business plan through a believable flow.

ideas.idea: Built for the long haul: no lock-in, revoke in one click, your mail never leaves your provider's storage.
ideas.why: Low commitment lowers the fear of trying it.

ideas.idea: What it won't do: the page opens with restraints (won't store your mail, won't send unapproved when approval is on) and only then lists what it does.
ideas.why: Restraint is the product's selling point for cautious buyers.

ideas.idea: Provider-first: 'Which inbox do you use?' picker at the top; the steps and notes below adapt to the chosen provider.
ideas.why: Every visitor reads their own setup story.

ideas.idea: Velocity story: the product told through what shipped recently, with dated changelog entries as chapters.
ideas.why: Shows an active product without inventing numbers.

ideas.idea: Interview: the page as a Q and A with the maker; questions in bold, short honest answers.
ideas.why: Conversational, human, answers objections in passing.

ideas.idea: Install-led: start from 'You already use Claude or ChatGPT', show the install, then what to ask first.
ideas.why: Matches visitors who arrive from client directories.

ideas.idea: A 'Works with' wall of supported providers and clients, each linking to its setup guide; labelled as compatibility, never 'trusted by'.
ideas.why: Real, checkable, and it answers fit.

ideas.idea: Security model block with four plain statements: mail fetched live and never stored, credentials encrypted at rest, OAuth access revocable in one click, data stored in Stockholm.
ideas.why: The four facts people actually ask about, stated plainly.

ideas.idea: The approval flow as proof: three real screenshots of the draft card (draft, held for approval, sent).
ideas.why: Shows the safety mechanism instead of claiming it.

ideas.idea: Changelog pace: the latest dated entries read from the public changelog at build time, linking to the full page.
ideas.why: Real dates prove an active product.

ideas.idea: Real customer quotes only, each with a name and a link to where it was published; the section is hidden when there are none approved.
ideas.why: Avoids invented testimonials entirely.

ideas.idea: Data location as a plain label: 'Data stored in Stockholm, Sweden', linking to the sub-processor list.
ideas.why: A concrete, verifiable fact for EU buyers.

ideas.idea: Open by default: links to the public GitHub repository, the npm package and the docs, with 'read the code' as a secondary link.
ideas.why: Anyone can check how it works.

ideas.idea: Sub-processor list summarised on the homepage (name and what each does), linking to the full page.
ideas.why: Business buyers check this before signing up.

ideas.idea: Listings in public MCP directories, linked out to the actual listing pages.
ideas.why: Third-party presence that visitors can verify.

ideas.idea: Install screenshots inside each client's connector settings (Claude, ChatGPT), showing the real connector entry.
ideas.why: Proves the integration is real, not a mockup.

ideas.idea: Full pricing table on the homepage, including Business per person, with no 'contact us' gate.
ideas.why: Transparency is proof of good faith.

ideas.idea: Company details in the footer: legal entity name, address and a real support address.
ideas.why: A real company behind the product.

ideas.idea: Revoke demo: a screenshot of the revoke control and one line on what stops working immediately.
ideas.why: Shows the user can always pull the plug.

ideas.idea: OAuth scopes shown verbatim per provider (what Gmail and Microsoft ask for), with a one-line plain-English reading of each.
ideas.why: Radical clarity about access.

ideas.idea: Self-host option as proof: a short note that the stack is available to self-host with Docker, linking to the guide.
ideas.why: If you can run it yourself, the hosted version has nothing to hide.

ideas.idea: Commitments list: 14-day refund, cancel any time, revoke any time, export or delete your account.
ideas.why: Plain promises that lower the risk of trying.

ideas.idea: A named support contact: 'Questions go to support@, and a person answers', next to the founder's name.
ideas.why: Human support is real proof for a small company.

ideas.idea: Screenshots without browser chrome, 1px hairline border, captioned 'Fig. n' with one sentence each.
ideas.why: Keeps focus on the UI and reads as documentation.

ideas.idea: The 3D postbox appears once, as the anchor of the 'Connect your inbox' section, its slots labelled with provider names.
ideas.why: One strong object at the step it represents.

ideas.idea: The 3D draft card shown three times down the page: front (draft), edge-on (approval), back with a 'Sent' stamp (done).
ideas.why: One object carries the whole story arc.

ideas.idea: The how-it-works diagram as one full-width horizontal line across the page, each segment revealed as you reach it.
ideas.why: One diagram, read left to right, no icon grid.

ideas.idea: Provider logo wall as a mail-sorting cabinet: a grid of pigeonholes, one provider logo per hole, empty holes labelled 'any IMAP'.
ideas.why: Makes the logo wall a postal object instead of a strip.

ideas.idea: Only one clip on the page, in the hero; every other asset is a still.
ideas.why: Keeps the page calm and fast.

ideas.idea: Detail crops at 200%: the Approve button, the To field, the inbox picker, each with a numbered callout and short label.
ideas.why: Points at the exact controls that matter.

ideas.idea: Small 3D envelope renders used as step markers (1, 2, 3) in place of icons.
ideas.why: Ownable markers instead of generic icons.

ideas.idea: Before and after comparison of the same inbox: a raw inbox screenshot and one with drafts ready, with a draggable divider.
ideas.why: Shows the difference directly.

ideas.idea: Annotated dashboard: one large dashboard screenshot with numbered pins and a legend list below it.
ideas.why: Explains the control panel in one image.

ideas.idea: 3D objects shot like catalogue products with spec captions ('Material: TLS. Contents: read live, not kept.').
ideas.why: Playful but true captions turn props into proof.

ideas.idea: Diagrams in the margin: small line diagrams sit in the right margin next to the paragraph they explain.
ideas.why: Diagrams support the text instead of interrupting it.

ideas.idea: Connect screens as a contact sheet: a strip of small thumbnails of each provider's connect screen (Gmail OAuth, Outlook, iCloud app password).
ideas.why: Shows breadth of providers with real screens.

ideas.idea: Screenshots on cream mats with museum-style labels (title, date shipped, short note).
ideas.why: Treats the product as something made with care.

ideas.idea: Chat and inbox side by side, joined by a hairline that connects the message in the chat to the same message in the inbox.
ideas.why: Makes 'live, not copied' visible.

ideas.idea: Clips that play only on hover or focus, with a still poster frame by default.
ideas.why: Motion only when asked for.

ideas.idea: A single 3D object in the hero, then none again; the rest of the page uses real screenshots only.
ideas.why: Lets the object be memorable without becoming decoration.

ideas.idea: No motion at all: a static page with designed hover underlines and focus rings only.
ideas.why: Calm, fast, accessible.

ideas.idea: Each section fades up 8px once on entry (200ms), disabled under prefers-reduced-motion.
ideas.why: Gentle rhythm without distraction.

ideas.idea: One looping hero clip that pauses when off screen, with visible pause control.
ideas.why: Motion where it explains, nowhere else.

ideas.idea: Hovering the Approve button on the draft card turns it into 'Sent 09:14' with a mint check, and back on leave.
ideas.why: Lets visitors feel the approval moment.

ideas.idea: The how-it-works line draws itself once as it enters view (SVG stroke offset), then stays.
ideas.why: Draws attention to the data path once.

ideas.idea: The 3D object idles with a very slow 6-degree turn only while in view, and stops under reduced motion.
ideas.why: Adds life to the object without stealing focus.

ideas.idea: Hovering a provider logo reveals how it connects (OAuth or app password) in a small label below it.
ideas.why: Useful detail on demand.

ideas.idea: A chapter number in the left margin updates as you scroll through sections.
ideas.why: Orientation for a long page.

ideas.idea: Before and after screenshot crossfade on a slow 5-second loop, paused on hover.
ideas.why: Shows change over time with no interaction needed.

ideas.idea: The envelope flap lifts slightly when the Start free button is hovered.
ideas.why: A small delight tied to the main action.

ideas.idea: Copy feedback on the connector URL: 'Copied' replaces the button label for two seconds.
ideas.why: Functional motion that confirms an action.

ideas.idea: Linked FAQ answers get a brief cobalt-soft background flash when reached by anchor.
ideas.why: Helps people land on the right answer.

ideas.idea: Client tabs: only the underline slides between Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and VS Code.
ideas.why: Minimal motion on an interactive control.

ideas.idea: Screenshots reveal with a one-time left-to-right clip-path wipe on entry.
ideas.why: A print-like reveal that suits left-aligned layout.

ideas.idea: An 'APPROVED' stamp settles from 1.08 to 1.0 scale with a small rotation once when the draft card enters view.
ideas.why: Gives the approval idea a single memorable beat.

ideas.idea: A thin cobalt reading-progress line in the left index of the long-read.
ideas.why: Calm orientation, no scroll hijack.

ideas.idea: A single message in the hero transcript 'arrives' (fades in) after a one-second pause on first load, then nothing else moves.
ideas.why: Feels live without fake typing.

ideas.idea: Hero (draft card) > Providers strip > How it works (Fig. 1 to 3) > Security model > Use cases by mailbox > Pricing > FAQ > Closing CTA
ideas.why: Leads with the differentiator, then fit, then trust.

ideas.idea: Type-only hero > Founder letter > Demo clip > Providers > Pricing > FAQ > Footer with company details
ideas.why: Human first, product second.

ideas.idea: Hero > Three objections answered > Demo > Teams on their own domain > Pricing > Install in Claude or ChatGPT > FAQ
ideas.why: Clears doubts before asking for anything.

ideas.idea: Masthead and lead story > Providers column > How it works > Latest changelog dispatches > Pricing > Colophon
ideas.why: Newspaper order for the newspaper layout.

ideas.idea: Hero clip > Connect (providers) > Paste URL (clients) > Ask > Approve > Sent > Pricing > FAQ
ideas.why: The page is the setup sequence.

ideas.idea: Hero > For you / For your team fork > Shared inboxes > Who approves > Security > Pricing (Business first) > FAQ
ideas.why: Puts the team buyer on equal footing.

ideas.idea: Index > 01 What it is > 02 Providers > 03 Clients > 04 Security > 05 Approval > 06 Plans > 07 Questions
ideas.why: Manual order, easy to jump around.

ideas.idea: Hero question > Answer card > How it got there (diagram) > What it can do > What it won't do > Pricing > Start free
ideas.why: Task first, mechanics second.

ideas.idea: Hero > Security first (never stored, Stockholm, encrypted, revoke) > Demo > Providers > Pricing > FAQ
ideas.why: For buyers whose first question is privacy.

ideas.idea: Hero > Use cases (invoices@, sales@, info@, personal) > Draft card demo > Providers > Clients > Pricing > Changelog > CTA
ideas.why: Leads with jobs to be done.

ideas.idea: Hero (provider list) > Pick your provider > Tailored setup steps > Client install > Approval > Pricing > FAQ
ideas.why: Personal setup path from the first click.

ideas.idea: Hero > By hand versus connected > Demo > Security > Pricing > FAQ
ideas.why: Comparison-led, short.

ideas.idea: Hero > Spec sheet > Fig. 1 dashboard > Fig. 2 draft card > Fig. 3 connect screens > Pricing table > Footnotes
ideas.why: Reference order for technical readers.

ideas.idea: Hero > Real quotes > Feature rows (alternating) > Letter > Pricing > Closing CTA
ideas.why: Proof early, story later.

ideas.idea: Hero > Install buttons (Claude, ChatGPT) > What to ask first (prompt list) > Providers > Security > Pricing > FAQ
ideas.why: Gets people from install to first useful prompt.

ideas.idea: Hero > Day in the life (morning, noon, evening) > Approval > Teams > Pricing > FAQ > Recent changelog
ideas.why: Habit story with a living-product ending.

ideas.idea: Short hero > FAQ as main body (Setup, Safety, Teams, Billing) > Pricing > Start free
ideas.why: Answer-led page for cautious visitors.

ideas.idea: Plain manual voice. Sample: 'Connect an inbox. Paste one URL. Ask.'
ideas.why: Short instructions match a short setup.

ideas.idea: Calm Scandinavian understatement. Sample: 'It reads your mail when you ask, and keeps none of it.'
ideas.why: Matches Stockholm and a privacy-first product.

ideas.idea: Opinionated and direct. Sample: 'Your AI writes good email. Let it send, once you say yes.'
ideas.why: Takes a clear position on agents and email.

ideas.idea: Small-maker warmth. Sample: 'This page is short because the setup is short.'
ideas.why: Human and honest without fake intimacy.

ideas.idea: Wry and self-aware. Sample: 'Yes, it works with the IMAP server your company set up in 2009.'
ideas.why: Disarms the most common fit worry with a smile.

ideas.idea: Precise technical. Sample: 'Mail is fetched from your provider when the AI asks for it, and it is not stored.'
ideas.why: Earns trust from developers and IT.

ideas.idea: Second-person reassurance. Sample: 'You see every draft before it leaves. You can change that later.'
ideas.why: Puts the reader in control in every sentence.

ideas.idea: Business-plain for teams. Sample: 'Give the AI the invoices@ inbox. Keep the approve button for yourself.'
ideas.why: Speaks to owners delegating shared inboxes.

ideas.idea: Literary and spare. Sample: 'An inbox is a list of small promises. This helps you keep them.'
ideas.why: Lifts a utility into something people care about.

ideas.idea: Clipped fragments. Sample: 'Ask. Review. Send.'
ideas.why: Fast to scan, easy to remember.

ideas.idea: FAQ plainness. Sample: 'Does it store my email? No. It fetches it when asked.'
ideas.why: Answers in the reader's own words.

ideas.idea: Mission voice. Sample: 'Your mail belongs in your mailbox, not in one more database.'
ideas.why: Frames privacy as a principle, not a feature.

ideas.idea: Newspaper headlines. Sample: 'Inbox answers itself; owner approves every reply.'
ideas.why: Fits the newspaper layout and makes features newsworthy.

ideas.idea: Postal and playful. Sample: 'We carry the letter. We don't keep a copy.'
ideas.why: A memorable metaphor that is also the privacy promise.

ideas.idea: Two readers, human and agent: sections for people with a short aside to the AI. Sample: 'Note to the agent: ask before you send.'
ideas.why: Acknowledges that agents read pages too.

ideas.idea: Modest and concrete. Sample: 'A small company, a real inbox for support, and nothing of yours on our disks.'
ideas.why: No hype, just facts a buyer can check.

ideas.idea: Field-guide description. Sample: 'iCloud: connects with an app password. Found in personal and family inboxes.'
ideas.why: Matter-of-fact entries make provider fit easy.

ideas.idea: One colour only: every element in brand cobalt on white, screenshots duotoned to cobalt and paper.
ideas.why: Forces hierarchy through size and space; strong brand recall.

ideas.idea: No images above the fold: type only; the first image is the draft card just below the fold.
ideas.why: Confidence and speed.

ideas.idea: The page is a printed letter: letterhead, date, 'Dear reader,', a signature, and Start free as the P.S.
ideas.why: Mail product, mail form.

ideas.idea: Every section is an email: each one has a From / To / Subject / Date header block and a body.
ideas.why: The product's medium becomes the page's grammar.

ideas.idea: The whole homepage lives inside one huge draft card frame, and the CTA is its Approve button.
ideas.why: The page itself demonstrates approval.

ideas.idea: Only three font sizes on the whole page.
ideas.why: Discipline that produces calm.

ideas.idea: Everything aligns to an 80-character monospace grid with plain text rules, no terminal chrome.
ideas.why: Developer-native and precise.

ideas.idea: The top of the page is an envelope front: an address block 'To: you@yourcompany.com', a stamp, a Stockholm postmark; the content follows below like an unfolded letter.
ideas.why: Ownable and on-theme without scroll tricks.

ideas.idea: All copy fits in 300 words; screenshots carry the rest.
ideas.why: Forces clarity.

ideas.idea: Footnotes for every claim: superscript numbers link to the docs or changelog entry that proves it.
ideas.why: Every statement is checkable.

ideas.idea: Providers drawn as numbered field-guide plates I to XII.
ideas.why: Turns the logo wall into an artefact.

ideas.idea: Every visual carries a museum label with real metadata (what it is, date it shipped).
ideas.why: Proof built into captions.

ideas.idea: The page is a manual's table of contents; every line expands into its section in place.
ideas.why: One screen holds the whole product.

ideas.idea: No top navigation bar at all; a left index is the only navigation.
ideas.why: Removes the generic SaaS header.

ideas.idea: Each section header shows the date it was last updated, taken from git.
ideas.why: Shows the page is maintained.

ideas.idea: Lowercase everywhere except product and provider names.
ideas.why: A distinct, quiet voice in type.

ideas.idea: The page is printable: a print stylesheet turns it into a two-page A4 brief a manager can hand on.
ideas.why: Business buyers often forward the page to a boss.
